# NVIDIA OpenShell as a Security Boundary for Agentic Tool Usage

Research Date: 2026-03-28
28 sources cited | 31 source pages fetched | 8 research dimensions

---

## 1. Executive Summary

NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source (Apache 2.0 [20]) runtime that enforces
security policies on AI coding agents through out-of-process, kernel-level
mechanisms. Launched March 16, 2026 at GTC, it addresses a fundamental
limitation of in-process security models like Claude Code hooks: "once control
passes to a subprocess, the application has no visibility into or control over
the subprocess" [9].

OpenShell substantially mitigates four of the six critical gaps identified in
the [security-skills research](../security-skills/): command encapsulation
bypass, regex evasion, TOCTOU, and config file weaponization. It partially
mitigates data exfiltration through deny-by-default network egress. It does not
address prompt injection — by design.

**Key finding**: OpenShell is architecturally sound but operationally immature.
It is developer-preview software with no third-party security audit, no
regulated-industry deployments, and sandbox implementation "untested under
real-world adversarial conditions" [20]. For a developer workstation running
Claude Code with the Anthropic API, it is viable today on any machine with
Docker and at least 4 GB RAM — ~2.0-2.5 GB (est.) for the stack plus headroom
for OS and agent. No GPU required. For production use, it is premature.

## 2. What Is OpenShell

OpenShell is a governance layer between AI agents and infrastructure,
implementing four enforcement domains [2]:

| Domain | Mechanism | Enforcement Timing |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|
| Filesystem | Landlock LSM (kernel) | Locked at creation [3] |
| Process | seccomp BPF + unprivileged UID | Locked at creation [3] |
| Network | HTTP CONNECT proxy + OPA/Rego | Hot-reloadable [3] |
| Inference | Privacy router (inference.local) | Hot-reloadable [7] |

The architecture comprises four components: Gateway (control plane + auth),
Sandbox (isolated runtime), Policy Engine (filesystem/network/process
enforcement), and Privacy Router (LLM routing) [1].

Agents run inside sandboxes with deny-by-default posture — no filesystem
access outside declared paths, no outbound network unless policy allows, no
root privileges, no dangerous syscalls [2][3]. Policies are declarative YAML;
network policies can be updated live without recreating the sandbox [5].

Three deployment models: Local (Docker on workstation), Remote (via SSH), and
Cloud (behind reverse proxy) [1].

Full architecture details: [architecture.md](references/architecture.md)

## 3. Policy Model Deep Dive

Policies are YAML with four sections [3]:

**Static** (locked at sandbox creation, require destroy/recreate to change):
- `filesystem_policy`: Per-directory read-only and read-write paths. Deny-by-default.
  Max 256 paths, 4096 chars each, no `..` traversal, no root [3].
- `landlock`: Compatibility mode (`best_effort` or `hard_requirement`) [3].
- `process`: Non-root user/group identity (default: `sandbox`) [3].

**Dynamic** (hot-reloadable):
- `network_policies`: Named blocks mapping binaries to endpoints. Per-binary,
  per-host, per-port at L4; per-method/path at L7 when `protocol: rest` [3].
  Access levels: `full`, `read-only` (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS), `read-write`
  (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/POST/PUT/PATCH) [3].

Default policy: Full coverage for Claude Code, partial for OpenCode, none for
Codex [4]. "If you run a non-Claude agent without a custom policy, the agent's
API calls are denied by the proxy" [4].

Inference routing via `inference.local`: strips sandbox credentials, injects
backend credentials. Single provider-model per gateway. Supports NVIDIA,
OpenAI-compatible, and Anthropic-compatible providers [7].

Full policy details: [policy-model.md](references/policy-model.md)

## 4. Threat Model Analysis

Mapped against the six gaps from the [security-skills research](../security-skills/):

| Gap | Status | Mechanism | Residual Risk |
|-----|--------|-----------|---------------|
| 1. Command encapsulation bypass | **Substantially addressed** | Landlock + per-binary network policy cover all subprocesses [9][3] | Overly broad binary globs; `best_effort` degradation |
| 2. Regex evasion | **Substantially addressed** | Enforces at syscall/TCP level, not string matching [3] | URL encoding evasion in L7 glob; DNS rebinding |
| 3. TOCTOU | **Partially addressed** | Landlock continuous kernel enforcement eliminates filesystem TOCTOU [12] | Network policy proxy may have brief TOCTOU during hot-reload |
| 4. Data exfiltration | **Partially addressed** | Deny-by-default egress with L7 access levels [3][9] | DNS exfil, URL parameter leaks, inference content, Git push |
| 5. Prompt injection | **Not addressed** | By design — reduces blast radius only [13] | Full residual risk; injected prompts operate within sandbox constraints |
| 6. Config weaponization | **Substantially addressed** | Filesystem policy can protect config paths [9][3] | Requires explicit configuration; defaults unclear |

**New threats introduced**: Landlock kernel bypass (Landlock requires Linux 5.13+), Docker
shared-kernel container escape [21], undocumented seccomp filter list [5],
policy misconfiguration (gateway on 0.0.0.0 [13], audit mode persistence [3]),
hot-reload as attack surface [5].

Full threat analysis: [threat-model-coverage.md](references/threat-model-coverage.md)

## 5. Comparison: Out-of-Process vs In-Process Security

| Dimension | Claude Code Hooks | OpenShell |
|-----------|------------------|-----------|
| Subprocess coverage | None [9] | Full (kernel-level) |
| Bypass resistance | Low (regex evasion) | High (syscall/TCP level) |
| TOCTOU | Check-then-execute gap | Continuous enforcement |
| Developer friction | Low | Medium (sandbox lifecycle) |
| Performance overhead | Negligible | Low-moderate (proxy + Landlock) |
| Maturity | Production | Developer preview [20] |

OpenShell's isolation is weaker than hardware-backed alternatives [21]:

| Technology | Isolation | Startup | Overhead | Recommendation |
|------------|-----------|---------|----------|----------------|
| Firecracker MicroVM | Hardware (hypervisor) | ~125ms | <5 MiB | "For production AI agents executing untrusted code" [21] |
| Kata Containers | Hardware (VMM) | ~200ms | Minimal | Regulated industries, zero-trust [21] |
| gVisor | User-space kernel | <1ms | 10-30% I/O | Multi-tenant, compute-heavy [21] |
| OpenShell | Kernel LSM + proxy | Container startup | ~2 GB RAM | Developer workstation, single-tenant |
| Docker (plain) | Process (shared kernel) | <1ms | Minimal | Trusted code only [21] |

AARTS v0.1 [22] and OpenShell are complementary: AARTS covers application-layer
hooks (prompt inspection, skill loading, memory operations) that OpenShell
cannot reach; OpenShell covers kernel-level enforcement that AARTS
implementations cannot guarantee.

Full comparison: [security-model-comparison.md](references/security-model-comparison.md)

## 6. Agent Integration Patterns

OpenShell wraps agents without code changes [8]. Deployment:

```bash
openshell sandbox create --policy ./my-policy.yaml -- claude
```

Credential management via privacy router: "Strips original credentials from
sandbox requests" and "Injects configured backend credentials" [7]. Sandboxes
don't need API keys.

**Agent agnostic claim**: Architecturally valid — enforces at OS level
regardless of agent internals. Operationally limited — Claude Code is the only
agent with full out-of-box default policy support [4].

Single provider-model pairing per gateway constrains multi-model workflows [7].

Full details: [agent-compatibility.md](references/agent-compatibility.md)

## 8. Developer Workstation Fit

**Fedora Linux**: K3s supports Fedora [23]. Requires Docker (not Podman) [6].

**Resource impact** on a 16 GB laptop:
- K3s server: ~1.6 GB RAM, 6% CPU (Intel server baseline) [24]
- OpenShell overhead: 300-800 MB (est.) — no profiling data published
- Total: ~2.0-2.5 GB (est.), ~10% of 16 GB

**Policy latency**: OPA RBAC benchmark ~45 µs [26]. Imperceptible vs Anthropic
API round-trip (500ms-5s).

**IDE integration**: VS Code Remote-SSH to sandbox. No native extension.

**Remote gateway**: `--remote user@host` deploys K3s + sandbox on a separate
machine, keeping the laptop thin [8].

Full details: [workstation-applicability.md](references/workstation-applicability.md)

## 9. Hardware Requirements

**No GPU required** for Claude Code + Anthropic API. GPU hardware is for local
inference (Nemotron) [8][19].

### Resource Budget

| Component | CPU | RAM | Storage |
|-----------|-----|-----|---------|
| K3s server (SQLite) | 6% of host CPU [24] | 1596 MB [24] | SSD, 10 IOPS [24] |
| Docker engine | negligible | ~49 MB [25] | ~1 GB images (est.) |
| OpenShell containers | unknown | 300-800 MB (est.) | unknown |
| **Combined floor** | **~0.5 cores (est.)** | **~2.0-2.5 GB (est.)** | **SSD, ~10 GB (est.)** |

### Homelab Viability

| Hardware | Viable? | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| Intel NUC (11+) | **Yes** | Ideal — 16-32 GB, NVMe |
| SFF PC (Optiplex) | **Yes** | Equivalent to NUC |
| Old laptop (2018+, SSD) | **Likely yes** | 8 GB tight, 16 GB fine |
| Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB) | **Marginal** | External SSD mandatory [23]; 30% CPU for K3s alone [24] |
| Raspberry Pi 4 | **Unlikely** | 4 GB insufficient; 8 GB possible with ext SSD |

## 10. Recommendations

### For a Developer Workstation (Claude Code + Anthropic API)

1. **Use OpenShell today for defense-in-depth** alongside Claude Code hooks.
   The combination provides both application-layer prompt inspection (hooks)
   and kernel-level enforcement (OpenShell). Neither is sufficient alone [9][22].

2. **Start with the default policy** — it has full Claude Code support [4].
   Iterate using the hot-reload workflow to tune network policies [5].

3. **Set `landlock.compatibility: hard_requirement`** for security-critical
   work. `best_effort` silently degrades on older kernels [3][5].

4. **Protect agent config files** explicitly in filesystem policy. Place
   `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json` in `read_only` paths.

5. **Use the remote gateway pattern** (`--remote user@host`) to offload K3s
   overhead to a homelab server. An Intel NUC with 16 GB RAM and NVMe SSD is
   the ideal minimum hardware.

### For Production Deployment

6. **Do not use OpenShell as a sole security boundary in production.** It is
   developer-preview software with no third-party audit [20]. Layer it with
   Firecracker/Kata for stronger isolation [21].

7. **Evaluate Cisco DefenseClaw** for operational governance [16][17]. It adds
   skill scanning, MCP inspection, and behavioral monitoring that OpenShell
   does not provide.

8. **Wait for**: third-party security audit, stable policy schema, multi-tenant
   support, and at least one regulated-industry reference deployment [20].

## 11. Limitations and Gaps

### Data Gaps in This Research

| Gap | Impact |
|-----|--------|
| OpenShell resource profiling | Cannot provide precise hardware sizing |
| regorus (Rust Rego) benchmarks | Policy evaluation latency is estimated, not measured |
| Seccomp filter list | Cannot assess syscall-level coverage |
| Default policy for agent configs | Cannot confirm config weaponization protection |
| Microsoft Defender comparison | Source failed to fetch [28] |

### Fundamental Limitations of the OpenShell Approach

- **Prompt injection is unsolvable at runtime** [10][13] — OpenShell reduces
  blast radius but cannot prevent model compromise
- **Covert channel exfiltration** (DNS, URL parameters, inference content)
  is not addressed by network policy enforcement
- **Shared-kernel isolation** inherits Docker's container escape risk [21] —
  weaker than Firecracker/Kata
- **Policy misconfiguration** is the primary operational risk — gateways
  exposed on 0.0.0.0 [13], audit mode left enabled [3], overly broad paths
- **Single-tenant only** — "not a supported multi-tenant hostile boundary" [13]
- **Full lifecycle not covered** — "agent security does not begin at the
  runtime layer" [20]; supply chain, development, and deployment governance
  require additional tooling

### Source Limitations

- 2 of 28 sources failed to fetch (Trend Micro 403 [18], VentureBeat 429 [27]);
  data supplemented via WebSearch snippets
- 1 source returned metadata only (Microsoft Defender [28])
- NVIDIA documentation is first-party with no independent verification
- Penligent and Snyk findings target OpenClaw, not OpenShell directly — OpenShell
  assessment is partially inferential
- No academic peer-reviewed analysis of OpenShell was found in searches
  (12 days post-launch at time of research)
